title: Grand swirls
caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 1566, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA Acknowledgement: Flickr user Det58

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The tiny yet intensely bright nucleus of NGC 1566 glitters at the center of this Hubble image, framed by swirling, symmetrical lavender arms. According to the caption, the galaxy is about 40 million light-years away, in Dorado, the Dolphinfish.

It is classed as an intermediate spiral, which lacks a clearly defined bar of stars at its center but is not quite an unbarred spiral either. Its tiny, brilliant core marks it as a Seyfert galaxy, a type whose centers are very active and luminous, sending out strong bursts of radiation and possibly hosting supermassive black holes that outweigh the Sun many millions of times over.
Among known Seyfert galaxies, it ranks second in brightness. It also outshines and dominates every other member of the Dorado Group, one of the richest galaxy groups in the southern hemisphere.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3. The source lists filters from the ultraviolet to the near-infrared. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Parts of this data lie in ultraviolet and near-infrared light, which the eye cannot see.
